zone: Darrington — Squire Creek and Clear Creek
_areas_note: The honest finding, stated by the research and kept: Squire Creek Wall, Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress are DAY CLIMBING from the car on short steep climbers' trails. There is no established high camp serving any of them, so these entries are valley campgrounds, dispersed roadside camping and on-route ledges rather than approach bivouacs. Whitehorse Mountain and Mount Higgins were flagged as NOT belonging to this approach and are not in the declared area, whose subtree is Northern Section / Waterfall Basin / Illusion Wall / South Face.

sites.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
sites.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable
sites.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
sites.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
sites.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.

sites.name: Clear Creek Campground
sites.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft
sites.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
sites.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
sites.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.

sites.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
sites.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most
sites.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
sites.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
sites.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.

sites.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
sites.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
sites.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
sites.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.

sites.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
sites.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
sites.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.

sites.name: Squire Creek Pass
sites.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass
sites.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
sites.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
sites.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
